name: Semma
description: Chef Vijay Kumar's celebrated West Village restaurant spotlights rare South Indian regional cooking rarely seen in the US, from Tamil Nadu and Kerala coastal traditions to Chettinad spice blends. The narrow, warmly lit dining room draws long waits, but 12 bar seats offer a walk-in option for the persistent.

name: Atomix
description: Junghyun and Ellia Park's intimate 14-seat counter in a NoMad townhouse reinterprets Korean culinary memory through a 10-course tasting menu, with each dish accompanied by a handwritten card telling the personal story behind it. One of NYC's most intellectually ambitious fine dining experiences, now priced at $385 per person.
popular_dishes: Ganjang Gejang (marinated crab with seaweed rice)
Aehobak (zucchini with lotus tea dashi and king crab)
Ganjang Quail Egg in seaweed shell with uni
Golden Eye Snapper with abalone egg jjim

name: Le Bernardin
description: Eric Ripert's legendary Midtown seafood temple has held three Michelin stars for decades, offering hushed luxury dining where precisely cooked fish is allowed to speak for itself in preparations that manage to feel both effortless and technically extraordinary. The four-course prix fixe at $218 per person spans sections named Almost Raw, Barely Touched, and Lightly Cooked.

name: Kabawa
description: Paul Carmichael's Caribbean-inspired tasting counter in the East Village occupies the former Momofuku Ko space and serves a three-course prix fixe at $145 with soca music bouncing off the walls and cooks in tie-dye aprons. The festive atmosphere and island-inflected dishes make it one of NYC's most joyful fine dining experiences of 2025.
popular_dishes: Roti Bread Course with curried channa and pepper jelly

name: Ha's Snack Bar
description: This tiny, perpetually fogged-up Lower East Side wine bar from the Ha's Dac Biet team serves a nightly-changing chalkboard menu of French-Vietnamese small plates where fish sauce and bird's eye chilies thread through even the most familiar forms, from snails in tamarind butter to a cilantro-forward onion soup with pho-like broth. Walk-in seats at the bar are the primary way to dine; arrive by 4:45pm for the best odds.
popular_dishes: Snails with Garlic and Tamarind Butter
Branzino with Mam Nem and Peanuts

name: King
description: This intimate South Village restaurant from Annie Shi and chefs Clare de Boer and Jess Shadbolt serves a daily-changing menu of French and Italian-inflected Mediterranean cooking with immaculate technique and impeccably sourced seasonal produce. The formal white-tablecloth room and restrained playlist give it a quietly elegant character suited to a mature, wine-serious crowd.
popular_dishes: Malfaldi pasta with butter and sage
Roasted Halibut with beans and greens

name: Penny
description: The 31-seat counter-only seafood and wine bar above sister restaurant Claud offers an exceptional raw bar and refined cooked seafood in an atmosphere that feels both luxurious and easy, with a wine room stocked to the ceiling and chefs working in full view. Limited reservations go quickly, but early or late walk-in spots are often available day-of.
popular_dishes: Ice Box (oysters, clams, scallop, mussels, Argentinian red shrimp)
Oyster Pan Roast with puff pastry
Ice Cream Sandwich (sesame brioche, balsamic strawberry)

name: Sushi Sho
description: Chef Keiji Nakazawa, who pioneered his Tokyo original and later a Waikiki outpost, brings his meticulous omakase tradition to a small wooden room near Bryant Park, serving roughly 20 courses that emphasize classical techniques like ice-aging, vinegar curing, and koji-rice fermentation (izushi) with no blowtorches or gimmicks. The no-photography policy preserves the intimacy of a meal that can run $800 or more with okonomi add-ons.
popular_dishes: Dried herring roe on mullet roe

name: Szechuan Mountain House
address: 23 Saint Marks Pl, New York, NY 10003
description: The East Village outpost of a Flushing original, decorated to resemble a mountain cottage with wooden beams and a koi pond, dishes out boldly ma-la Sichuan cooking with theatrical flair and headset-wearing servers who run a tight, fast-paced floor. Beyond the numbing classics, the menu extends to organ meats, pickled-pepper frog legs, and a showpiece swing pork belly served on a hanging rack.
popular_dishes: Swing Pork Belly with garlic chili oil
Mao Xue Wang (duck blood, tripe, gizzard in chili broth)

name: Tatiana by Kwame Onwuachi
address: 10 Lincoln Center Plaza, New York, NY 10023
description: Chef Kwame Onwuachi's landmark Lincoln Center restaurant melds his Bronx upbringing with Nigerian, Creole, and Caribbean culinary roots into a joyful, Biggie-soundtracked dining room that transformed New York's big-night-out scene when it opened in 2022. A six-seat bar is available for walk-ins, and the kitchen's tight menu of curried goat patties, short rib pastrami suya, and bodega brownie ice cream has almost no skips.
popular_dishes: Mom Duke's Head-On Shrimp in Creole Butter

name: 188 Bakery Cuchifritos
description: A fluorescent-lit Bronx institution since 1983, this counter-service spot is a carnival of Puerto Rican pork cookery: crispy chicharron, stewed pig ears, garlicky mofongo with pernil, and a softball-sized papa rellena that earns repeat pilgrimages. Don't skip the rich, crumbly morcilla.

name: A&A Bake and Doubles
description: A Bed-Stuy institution for Trinidadian street food, A&A is a counter-service spot where the pillowy bara and well-seasoned chana in the doubles are among the neighborhood's most beloved bites. Grab a fry bake, a goat roti, or a doubles and eat it immediately at a table up front for maximum effect.

name: AbuQir Seafood
description: A small Egyptian seafood market and restaurant on Steinway Street where you browse a daily fish counter — tiger shrimp, whole fish, squid, and octopus — and tell the counter staff how you want it cooked. The Egyptian-spiced whole fish is a standout, and the smoky baba ghanoush is essential.

name: Aska
description: Chef Fredrik Berselius's two-Michelin-star tasting menu restaurant in a restored Williamsburg warehouse offers an immersive Nordic experience of 12-16 courses built around foraged Northeast ingredients and seasonal seafood, all served to just 10 tables by a team that also forages upstate together. At $375 per person, it is a serious and rewarding special-occasion destination.
popular_dishes: Lobster poached in shell butter with white asparagus foam

name: Atoboy
description: Junghyun Park's Korean-inspired Flatiron restaurant offers an accessible and inventive four-course prix fixe at $75 all-in (including gratuity), letting diners mix and match small plates from categories of sea urchin, beef tartare, pork belly, scallops, and more. A fried chicken supplement is available for $28.

name: Barbuto
description: Chef Jonathan Waxman's celebrated West Village neighborhood restaurant has been a New York institution for its seasonal California-Italian cooking fired in brick and wood ovens; the garage doors open in summer, and the roast chicken with salsa verde is one of New York's most iconic dishes. Reservations accepted but walk-ins are welcomed at the bar.
popular_dishes: JW roast chicken with salsa verde
Chitarra pasta with walnuts and Parmesan

name: Barney Greengrass
description: This Upper West Side appetizing shop has been a New York landmark since 1908, renowned for its smoked fish — particularly the Nova Scotia salmon, sturgeon, and sable — served alongside eggs, bagels, and classic Jewish deli accompaniments in a reliably chaotic weekend atmosphere. Cash only for in-person dining.
popular_dishes: Scrambled eggs with Nova Scotia salmon

name: Birria-Landia
description: A food truck under the Roosevelt Avenue subway tracks in Jackson Heights widely regarded as the city's finest birria, serving Tijuana-style slow-stewed beef in a four-item menu built around a deeply tangy, spiced consome that doubles as a dipping broth. The crispy orange tortillas dipped in consome before hitting the griddle are a masterclass in simplicity.

name: Borgo
description: Andrew Tarlow's first Manhattan restaurant (from the team behind Diner, Marlow and Sons, and She Wolf bread) is an elegant, white-tablecloth Nomad trattoria with wood-burning oven and a generously spaced dining room, best known for its timballo di anelletti — a gloriously rich pasta pie — and fried delicata squash drizzled with honey and chili oil.
popular_dishes: Timballo di anelletti (pasta pie with braised beef)
Fried delicata squash with honey and Calabrian chili
Chicories salad with pear and walnuts

name: Bridges
description: From a former Estela chef, Bridges is a coolly atmospheric New American restaurant in Chinatown where quietly complex dishes — a buttery comté and chanterelle tart, an impossibly silky uni custard, duck breast with XO sauce — draw a scene-conscious but food-serious crowd to a room that feels like the inside of a bank vault. One of NYC's best new restaurants of 2025.
popular_dishes: Roasted duck breast with XO sauce

name: Bungalow
description: Chef Vikas Khanna's lively East Village dining room celebrates the diverse culinary traditions of India's 28 states, with vibrant cocktails and contemporary dishes that have earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand. Walk-in spots are eagerly sought, with diners lining up early when reservations run out.
popular_dishes: Yogurt kebabs with kataifi pastry and mango coulis

name: Cafe Kestrel
description: A compact, warmly elegant European bistro in Red Hook where French-leaning cooking shines in a tight menu of terrines, salads, and carefully composed entrees. Michelin-listed, it punches well above its small footprint with dishes like duck leg confit with kumquats and a standout apricot cake.
popular_dishes: Duck leg confit with rutabaga puree and candied kumquats
Seafood terrine with creme fraiche and gaufrettes

name: Cafe Mado
description: A skylit all-day cafe in Prospect Heights that transitions from morning coffee and house-baked bread to refined evening small plates and handmade pasta, with a rotating seasonal menu driven by what's fresh. Michelin-listed and part of the Redwood Hospitality family (Oxalis, Place des Fetes).
popular_dishes: Pissaladiere with anchovies and caramelized onions
Glazed duck confit with watermelon radish

name: Carnitas Ramirez
description: A nose-to-tail Mexican spot in the East Village open Wednesday through Sunday, devoted to the whole-animal tradition of carnitas and slow-cooked pork in all its forms. The small, casual space draws a loyal crowd for its deeply flavored renditions of a street-food classic.

name: Casa Mono and Bar Jamón
description: A Michelin-starred Spanish tapas bar on Irving Place inspired by the Costa Brava, where adventurous proteins like sweetbreads and cockscombs share the menu with classic a la plancha preparations and a 600-bottle Spanish wine list. Its sister bar, Bar Jamon next door, pours Iberico ham and churros in an intimate standing-room setting.
popular_dishes: Arroz negro with fluke and piparra emulsion
Sweetbreads with fennel and marcona almond vinaigrette
Hand-carved Jamon Iberico de Pata Negra

name: Cervo's
description: A Michelin Bib Gourmand seafood restaurant on Canal Street celebrating the coastal traditions of the Iberian Peninsula, with a Northeast-sourced menu, Iberian coastal wines, and a welcoming high-energy room of mosaic tiles and wood paneling. Outdoor seats are walk-in only in season; indoor seats take reservations year-round.
popular_dishes: Seabream with crispy skin and Habanada peppers
Pea shoot salad with roasted hazelnuts and aged goat cheese
Marinated potatoes with fried rock shrimp

name: Chambers
description: A Michelin-listed TriBeCa spot beloved for its casual elegance, product-focused seasonal plates, and an exceptional wine program curated by Master Sommelier Pascaline Lepeltier, featuring back vintages and surprising value. The kitchen turns out refined small and large plates like honeynut squash agnolotti and seared Long Island fluke.
popular_dishes: Castelfranco salad with heirloom chicory and clothbound cheddar
Long Island fluke with shelling beans and preserved lemon

name: Chez Ma Tante
description: A Michelin-listed Greenpoint gem with a meat-forward, French-Canadian sensibility where pates, terrines, and porky dishes define the menu alongside bold pastas and a legendary brunch that draws long lines on weekends. Desserts like maple creme brulee and lemon tart are equally essential.
popular_dishes: Fennel sausage with cannellini beans and Pernod

name: Cho Dang Gol
description: A longtime Koreatown stalwart and Michelin Bib Gourmand winner where house-made soft tofu is the star, served in bubbling casseroles and stews alongside rustic Korean favorites like pajeon, bibimbap, and kimchi stir-fries. A warm, simply decorated room makes it a reliable choice for unpretentious, soul-satisfying cooking.
popular_dishes: Sauteed tofu trio with pork belly and kimchi

name: Chongqing Lao Zao
description: An authentic Chongqing-style hotpot restaurant in the heart of Flushing, where house-made tallow broth with hand-selected spices delivers the genuine ma-la numbing-spicy experience of the mountain city. Signature ingredients like beef tripe, goose intestine, and premium yellow throat set it apart from genericized versions.

name: Çka Ka Qëllu
description: Named for a phrase meaning 'what we happen to have,' this Belmont dining room doubles as a museum of 18th and 19th century Albanian artifacts collected by its owner, Ramiz, who opened the restaurant after finding no authentic Albanian food in NYC. The hearty, homey cooking covers classic dishes from Albania and Kosovo alongside hand-collected regional relics in glass cases lining the walls.
popular_dishes: Burek (golden-brown phyllo stuffed with soft cheese)
Sarma (cabbage rolls with ground veal, rice, and vegetables)

name: Claud
description: Sommelier Chase Sinzer and chef Joshua Pinsky's below-street-level East Village room pairs an ingredient-focused shared-plates menu with one of the more thoughtful natural wine lists in the city. Reservations are competitive but the bar is always walk-in, making it a reliable evening anchor for the neighborhood.
popular_dishes: Red shrimp with garlic and olive oil
Pork chop with smoked onion jus

name: Cocina Consuelo
description: A husband-and-wife-run neighborhood spot in Hamilton Heights serving seasonal Mexican cooking with a festive sunlit room in yellow and blue, frequent live music, and a strict all-Mexican beer and wine list. The kitchen's 15-hour birria bone marrow and housemade corn tortillas anchor a menu that changes with the seasons.
popular_dishes: Birria bone marrow (15-hour braise, with salsa roja and housemade tortillas)
Shaved fennel salad with chayote and pickled grapes
Tres leches cake with heirloom corn and Mexican vanilla

name: Court Street Grocers
description: A beloved Carroll Gardens sandwich counter sourcing from high-quality regional producers to build both classic and inventive deli-style sandwiches, from a garlic-bread pork shoulder with duck sauce to a crispy-onion Boston-style roast beef. The daytime spot draws a loyal neighborhood crowd for breakfast egg sandwiches and lunch combos at approachable prices.
popular_dishes: Italian Combo (mortadella, soppressata, mozzarella on seeded hero)
Machin Man or Woman (pork shoulder, cheddar, pickled jalapenos, duck sauce)
The Reuben (corned short rib or turkey, sauerkraut)
American Combo (roast turkey, heritage ham, coleslaw)

name: Crown Shy
description: Chef James Kent's one-Michelin-star restaurant in the landmarked Art Deco 70 Pine Street tower combines soaring ceilings, marble floors, and a lively bar with an approachably creative American menu that moves effortlessly from Gruyere fritters to sizzling roasted short rib. Under current executive chef Jassimran Singh, the menu now weaves in South Asian flavors including a standout tandoori flatbread.
popular_dishes: Roasted short rib with couscous and ras el hanout sauce
Tomatoes and peaches in citrus vinaigrette with anchovy
Sticky toffee pudding with apple sorbet

name: Daniel
description: Daniel Boulud's one-Michelin-star flagship on the Upper East Side has been a fixture of New York fine dining for over thirty years, offering multicourse French tasting menus in a formal dining room adorned with art and Bernardaud porcelain chandeliers. Executive chef Eddy Leroux's seasonal compositions highlight pristine ingredients such as ikejima black cod with cauliflower cream and beluga lentils.
popular_dishes: Castroville artichoke ravioli with barigoule consomme
Pacific ikejima black cod with cauliflower cream and beluga lentils

name: Dera
description: A Jackson Heights dining room serving the overlapping cuisines of South Asia's four corners - Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, and Nepal - in a neighborhood that has long been one of the richest concentrations of that culinary tradition in New York. The menu spans tandoor-fired breads, biryanis, and slow-braised meats that reflect the diversity of the corridor along Roosevelt Avenue.

name: Dhamaka
description: Roni Mazumdar and chef Chintan Pandya's Michelin Bib Gourmand Indian restaurant at Essex Market is a bold love letter to the rustic, unapologetic cooking of India's hinterlands - offal, fierce heat, and clay pots are all part of the deal. The name means 'explosion' in Hindi, and the cooking delivers on that promise with dishes rarely seen in American Indian restaurants.
popular_dishes: Smoky goat belly with coriander seeds wrapped in cedar wood
Mutton in clay pot with dark chili oil and roasted garlic

name: Don Peppe
address: 135-58 Lefferts Blvd, South Ozone Park, NY 11420
description: A decades-old South Ozone Park institution beloved for its no-frills, generous red-sauce Italian-American cooking - the kind of place where regulars order off-menu and portions arrive family-style without ceremony. Located near JFK and largely off the Manhattan radar, it has long sustained a devoted local following who treat it as a neighborhood treasure.

name: Ewe's Delicious Treats
description: A Nigerian and West African bakery and restaurant in the New Lots neighborhood of Brooklyn, bringing the flavors of home cooking - egusi, jollof rice, suya, and puff-puff - to a part of Brooklyn that has historically had limited restaurant options. The operation runs on a small, personal scale that reflects the owner's commitment to the local community.

name: Eyval
description: A chic Bushwick offshoot of the acclaimed Prospect Heights Persian restaurant Sofreh, Eyval serves seasonal Iranian small plates in a bright, white-brick space adorned with LED Farsi lettering. The mood is cool but unstuffy, making it ideal for a stylish dinner of wagyu kebabs and potato tahdig without the formality.

name: The Four Horsemen
description: Co-owned by LCD Soundsystem's James Murphy, this treehouse-sized Williamsburg wine bar helped define the city's natural wine movement when it opened in 2015 and still sets the pace a decade later. Constantly rotating small plates — think sweetbreads, oeufs mayo, and butter beans in parmesan broth — pair with an 800-plus bottle list skewing low-intervention.
popular_dishes: Veal Sweetbread Skewers with soy-cured egg yolk
Celery Salad with dates and walnut

name: Four Twenty Five
description: Jean-Georges Vongerichten's bi-level dining room inside the striking 425 Park Avenue tower brings his signature global-French sensibility to Midtown's most polished new address. Expect leek-swirled foie gras terrine, sesame-crusted scallops, and duck breast with lemongrass-coconut sauce in a setting of dangling lights and a glass-enclosed kitchen.
popular_dishes: Foie Gras Terrine with spiced madeleines
Fluke Tartare with shiso and sea beans
Charred Duck Breast with lemongrass-coconut sauce

name: Frenchette
description: Lee Hanson and Riad Nasr, both Balthazar veterans, run this unfussy TriBeCa French bistro where the menu rotates daily and the butter content of every dish is non-negotiable. The worn wood floors and dim lighting make it feel like it has existed since before the internet, and the duck frites with bearnaise is among the most talked-about dishes in the city.

name: Gage & Tollner
description: A storied Downtown Brooklyn oyster and chop house that first opened in 1879, Gage and Tollner was resurrected in 2021 under new ownership who kept the grand chandeliers and red velvet booths while updating the kitchen. Its upstairs tiki bar, Sunken Harbor Club, has become a destination in its own right.

name: Golden Diner
description: Sam Yoo's diner in the Two Bridges neighborhood near Chinatown gives the classic American diner form a soulful Asian-American upgrade, serving all-day breakfast sandwiches on scallion milk buns alongside chicken katsu clubs and Thai cobb salads. Swivel stools, an analog clock, and lace curtains set the mood, but the food is anything but retro.
popular_dishes: Chinatown Breakfast Sandwich on scallion milk bun
Tuna Melt on grilled rye with salt-and-vinegar chips

name: Gramercy Tavern
description: Danny Meyer's iconic 1994 Gramercy landmark operates as two restaurants in one: a formal back dining room with a $175 seasonal tasting menu, and a lively walk-in tavern serving a legendary bacon-cheddar burger with duck fat chips and seasonal pastas. The tavern side is the sleeper hit, beloved by locals who skip the tasting entirely.
popular_dishes: Tavern Burger with bacon, cheddar, and duck fat chips
Chocolate Chip Cookie with cold milk

name: Great N.Y. Noodletown
description: A no-frills Chinatown cash-only institution that has been feeding night owls and noodle lovers for decades with roast meats and punchy Cantonese soups until the early hours. Service is brisk to the point of bluntness, the prices are low, and the wonton noodle soup and pan-fried beef chow fun are among the best in the city.

name: The Grill
description: Mario Carbone and Rich Torrisi's theatrical American restaurant inside the landmarked Seagram Building — where the term power lunch was invented — delivers an hours-long performance of tableside prime rib, pre-batched martinis poured from impossible heights, and a pasta sauce pressed from bones through an antique 1901 device. The room is dark, stage-lit wood, and the vibe is unabashedly expensive.
popular_dishes: Pasta a La Presse (antique presse bone-juice sauce)

name: Hainan Chicken House
description: A modern Malaysian hawker-style restaurant on the Sunset Park and Borough Park border that serves what many consider the best Hainanese chicken rice in the five boroughs, with poached chicken and fragrant rice presented on butcher paper to evoke the spirit of a Singapore hawker stall. Weekend specials on the whiteboard — sometimes Singapore Chili Crab — are worth planning around.
popular_dishes: Salted Duck Egg Yolk Crispy Prawns

name: Hamburger America
address: 155 West Houston St, New York, NY 10012
description: George Motz's love letter to the American hamburger, served counter-style from a tiny 15-stool diner in SoHo. The menu is unapologetically simple: smash burgers, cold beer, and classic diner sides in a nostalgic setting.

name: Hellbender
description: From a team of Gramercy Tavern alumni, Hellbender is a Mexican-American nighttime cafe tucked into Ridgewood, Queens, with a laid-back bar atmosphere, strong tequila and mezcal cocktails, and snacks rooted in the chef's Mexican heritage. The weekly rotating Jello dessert and chamoy-coated fruit have become neighborhood talking points.

name: Ho Foods
description: A closet-sized East Village gem specializing in Taiwanese beef noodle soup, with a slow-cooked broth that takes hours to build. The short menu of delicate tofu, minced pork over rice, and perfectly al-dente noodles punches well above the restaurant's modest footprint.
popular_dishes: Minced pork over rice (lu rou fan)

name: Houseman
description: Chef Ned Baldwin's neighborhood New American bistro in Hudson Square encourages family-style dining and builds menus around meticulously sourced, vibrant ingredients. The atmosphere is welcoming yet elegant, earning two stars from the New York Times for its exceptional whole roasted chicken and inventive vegetable preparations.

name: Jean-Georges
address: Trump International Hotel & Tower, 1 Central Park West, New York, NY 10023
description: Jean-Georges Vongerichten's flagship tasting menu restaurant at the Trump International Hotel overlooking Central Park holds two Michelin stars and is celebrated for masterful French technique infused with global influences. Chef de Cuisine Joseph Rhee maintains the restaurant's legacy of precision and elegance through constantly evolving seasonal menus.

name: Jeju Noodle Bar
description: A West Village Korean noodle bar drawing on the culinary traditions of Jeju Island, serving a creative interpretation of Korean comfort food rather than strictly traditional dishes. The intimate space fills quickly and the kitchen brings depth of flavor through house-made broths and seasonal accompaniments.

name: Jungsik
description: A three-Michelin-star Korean tasting menu restaurant in TriBeCa where Chef Yim Jung Sik and Executive Chef Daeik Kim deliver highly original Korean cuisine with impeccable technique, beginning with creative banchan presentations and unfolding through dishes like dry-aged Arctic char with kimchi and red curry sauce. The cool, polished dining room strikes a rare balance of downtown low-key and genuine elegance.
popular_dishes: Raw striped jack with white kimchi and chilled fish bone broth
Dry-aged Arctic char with kimchi and red curry sauce

name: Keens
description: A Midtown landmark since 1885, Keens is renowned for its legendary mutton chop, an extraordinary collection of 90,000 clay pipes hanging from the ceiling, and an encyclopedic Scotch whisky list. The historic dining room retains the character of the Herald Square Theatre District that once surrounded it.

name: Kisa
description: Kisa is a stripped-down Korean baekban diner on the Lower East Side modeled after the roadside diners of 1980s Korea, where $32 buys a protein, soup, rice, and seven bowls of banchan. Lunch is walk-in only; dinner reserves two-thirds of tables on Resy while keeping the rest for walk-ins, and the James Beard-nominated spot fills fast.

name: Koloman
description: Chef Markus Glocker's Viennese-influenced restaurant occupies the former Breslin space at the Ace Hotel in NoMad, blending Parisian creativity with Austrian tradition. The standout schnitzel Viennoise and impeccable gougeres anchor a menu that also features tafelspitz, terrines, and a well-curated list of spirit-free cocktails.

name: Kono
description: An intimate Japanese omakase counter that opened in Chinatown in 2025, offering a chef-driven tasting experience rooted in seasonal Japanese ingredients. The small-seat format and reservation-only policy make it one of the harder tables to land in the city.

name: Kopitiam
description: Chef-owner Kyo Pang, a third-generation Nyonya, serves fast-casual Nyonya cuisine in this coffee-shop-style spot on the Lower East Side, where no-reservations walk-ins order at the counter before seating. The menu highlights the hybrid Chinese-Malay cooking tradition with dishes made from scratch using Malaysian-sourced ingredients and no artificial additives.
popular_dishes: Nasi Lemak (coconut rice with ikan bilis, sambal, cucumber, egg)
Char Kway Teow (stir-fried flat rice noodles with shrimp and lap cheong)
Pan Mee (hand-pulled noodles in anchovy broth)
Kaya Butter Toast with Malaysian half-boiled eggs

name: Laghman Express
description: Brand chef Gulnoza Jurayeva has elevated Uyghur cuisine into a precision-run fast-casual concept in Brooklyn, with hand-pulled noodles at the center of a menu spanning Central Asian dumplings, grilled skewers, and spiced lamb dishes. The 20th Avenue Bensonhurst location is the flagship of a two-branch operation.
popular_dishes: Guyurou Laghman (hand-pulled noodles with lamb and vegetables)
Tashkent Plov (Uzbek rice pilaf with lamb and carrot)

name: Lakruwana
description: An exuberantly decorated Sri Lankan dining room in Stapleton where murals, sculptures, and flags cover every surface and the energetic owner works the floor personally. The menu centers on traditional street food and sharing platters, holding a Michelin recommendation for its bold, authentic flavors.
popular_dishes: Kottu roti (stir-fried godamba roti with chicken, vegetables, and curry)
Hoppers (bowl-shaped crepes with yellow fish curry)
Oversized sharing platter of Sri Lankan street food

name: Le Coucou
description: Chef Daniel Rose and restaurateur Stephen Starr bring refined French cuisine to a Roman and Williams-designed space in SoHo, where classic Parisian bistro cooking is executed with exceptional freshness and skill. The prix-fixe and a la carte menus span traditional dishes from quenelle de brochet to canette a l'orange.
popular_dishes: Quenelle de brochet (pike mousse with lobster sauce or beurre blanc)
Tout le lapin (all of the rabbit)

name: Le Veau d'Or
description: Originally opened in 1937 and revived by Balthazar-founding chefs Lee Hanson and Riad Nasr, this intimate prix-fixe bistro on the Upper East Side is a love letter to classic French cooking done impeccably. Dark wood, linen-draped tables, and unapologetically buttery sauces make it one of the most romantic rooms in the city.
popular_dishes: Poulet a l'estragon (roasted chicken with tarragon butter sauce)

name: Levant
description: A 2025 arrival in Astoria serving modern Middle Eastern cooking from the Levant region, with a menu that draws on the culinary traditions of Lebanon, Syria, and neighboring cuisines. Reservations are taken through Resy and the restaurant has attracted early buzz for its refined approach to the region's flavors.
popular_dishes: Mezze spread with seasonal dips and flatbreads

name: Lilia
description: Missy Robbins's celebrated Williamsburg restaurant pairs wood-fired seafood with handcrafted Italian pasta in a warm, convivial space that draws on regional Italian tradition and the spirit of countless Italian grandmothers. The pasta program is among the most acclaimed in NYC, with reservations notoriously hard to secure.
popular_dishes: Mafaldini with pink peppercorn and Parmigiano
Sheep's milk cheese agnolotti with saffron and honey
Rigatoni Diavola with San Marzano tomatoes

name: Little Myanmar
description: A family-run Burmese gem in the East Village where husband and wife team Thidar Kyaw and Tin Ko Naing serve a surprisingly large menu of soups, salads, curries, and roti dishes from a tiny room with outsized warmth. The Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized spot is known for bold flavors and generous portions perfect for sharing.
popular_dishes: Burmese pancake with vegetables and toasted sesame seeds
Kaut swe thoke (yellow noodle salad with chicken in curry sauce)

name: Lola's
description: Chef Suzanne Cupps's debut solo restaurant in NoMad weaves together her Filipino-American heritage, South Carolina upbringing, and years in elite NYC kitchens into shareable, ingredient-forward plates that range from gumbo roasted oysters to Carolina gold rice grit cakes. Walk-ins are accepted alongside Resy reservations.
popular_dishes: Gumbo roasted oysters with brown butter and chow chow relish
Southern barbecue short rib with baked beans and pickled collard greens
Heritage pork dumplings with tamarind and Thai basil
Housemade naan with carrot masala yogurt

name: Lucia Pizza of Avenue X
description: A slice shop on Avenue X in Sheepshead Bay that has quietly become one of Brooklyn's most celebrated pizzerias, known for a crust that threads the needle between floppy and crispy. Every pie is available by the slice and best eaten straight from the oven at one of the few tables inside.
popular_dishes: Caramelle Piccanti (spicy honey, cherry peppers, pepperoni cups)

name: Mắm
description: A Vietnamese restaurant on the edge of Chinatown where diners sit on low plastic stools and share herb-laden platters meant for dipping and rolling, rooted in the fermented fish-paste condiments that give the restaurant its name. The menu shifts with the seasons, from summer herb-and-pork bun dau platters to winter hot pots packed with catfish and pork.
popular_dishes: Bun Dau Dac Biet (pork belly, blood sausage, tofu, herbs platter)
Nam Cuon (mushroom rolling platter with fermented tofu sauce)
Oc Buou Nhoi Thit (apple snails stuffed with pork sausage)
Bun Hen (clam noodle soup with dill)

name: Okdongsik
description: A 13-seat counter in Koreatown devoted to a single dish: pork gomtang, a delicate clear-broth soup poured over rice in the gukbap tradition, served with kimchi and optional mandu. The light, clarifying soup and intimate format make it a destination for solo diners who want something quietly exceptional.
popular_dishes: Pork gomtang (clear pork bone soup over rice)

name: Okiboru House of Tsukemen
description: The New York outpost of this Japanese-trained tsukemen specialist serves cold noodles made from scratch alongside a thick, bonito-forward dipping broth that diners ladle over each strand before eating. The walk-in-only format keeps lines moving, and a soupy ramen option with milky pork-bone broth rounds out the tight menu.

name: Old Sport
description: A Chinese-American halal restaurant on Austin Street in Forest Hills that draws a devoted local crowd for its roast meats and layered rice dishes prepared with halal techniques. The casual storefront format and accessible pricing make it one of the more talked-about new spots to open in Queens in 2025.

name: Raf's
description: A Noho bistro from chefs Mary Attea and pastry chef Camari Mick, set inside a room painted with billowy clouds, whose French- and Italian-accented menu leans into perfectly executed classics: herb-laden roast chicken, hand-rolled pastas, and an essential white chocolate budino to finish. Reservations are competitive, but the bar is available for walk-ins.
popular_dishes: Carta di musica with jambon de Bayonne and Parmigiano

name: Raku
description: The East Village sibling of the acclaimed Soho original, Raku is a no-frills udon shop where thick, chewy noodles arrive in broths ranging from a spicy miso-based tantan to a refreshing cold yamakake with mountain yam. Cash only, unfussy, and ideal for a quick solo meal or low-key date.
popular_dishes: Tantan udon (spicy miso broth with pork)

name: Randazzo's Clam Bar
description: A Sheepshead Bay waterfront institution of more than 75 years, Randazzo's has anchored the Emmons Avenue promenade with its neon lobster sign and spicy secret-recipe tomato sauces ladled over fresh clams and calamari. The relaxed atmosphere and modest prices make it a perennial local favorite after a stroll along the bay.
popular_dishes: Raw clams on the half shell

name: S & P Lunch
description: A diner-style lunch counter that has faithfully carried on the legacy of Eisenberg's, the beloved sandwich shop that occupied this narrow Flatiron space since 1929, keeping swiveling counter stools, vinyl banquettes, and an expansive menu of classic New York deli and diner staples. It closes at 5pm daily, making it a breakfast and lunch destination only.

name: Sailor
description: A maritime-themed Fort Greene bistro from chef April Bloomfield where the menu reads like classic NYC bistro but executes with exceptional richness: a caesar drowning in paint-thick dressing, branzino heaped with charred-lemon relish, and a cult-favorite roast chicken served alongside parm-crusted potatoes soaked in jus. A 2025 expansion added a more casual bar room with a separate lamb burger.
popular_dishes: Roasted half chicken with parm-crusted potatoes
Whole branzino with charred lemon relish

name: Salty Lunch Lady's Little Luncheonette
description: Owner Dria Atencio's cheerful pastel luncheonette in Ridgewood turns out playful, creative sandwiches like a mortadella with aged provolone and ajvar pepper paste, alongside chicken meatball subs with Bulgarian feta. The dessert case — rotating layer cakes and pies — has built its own cult following.
popular_dishes: Chicken Meatball Sandwich with Bulgarian feta

name: Shaw-naé's House
address: 387 Van Duzer St, Staten Island, NY 10301
description: Chef Shaw-nae Dixon's intimate six-table soul food dining room in Stapleton Heights offers a meticulously personal experience where soulful, seasonal cooking — think smothered turkey wings and jerk chicken — feels like being welcomed into someone's home. With limited seating, every meal is deliberately warm and memorable.

name: Shukette
description: Chef Ayesha Nurdjaja's Chelsea follow-up to Shuka is a bright, rip-and-dip Middle Eastern feast built around exceptional breads — a garlicky frena and za'atar-showered lafa — paired with a rotating cast of dips and bold wood-fired main plates. Reservations are tough to snag and walk-in waits can stretch an hour or two, but the tahini soft serve alone is worth it.
popular_dishes: Fish In A Cage (whole grilled porgy with green charmoula)

name: Sofreh
description: Chef Nasim Alikhani's Prospect Heights Persian restaurant forgoes the usual kebab platters in favor of beautifully composed small plates — jewel-bright with pomegranate seeds, house-strained yogurt, and fresh herbs — drawing on the flavors she learned cooking as a child in Iran. The minimalist, modern dining room and the chef's habit of stopping by each table give every meal a personal, gracious warmth.
popular_dishes: Lamb Shank with butter beans and dried lime broth

name: Superiority Burger
description: Chef Brooks Headley's beloved East Village vegetarian diner operates out of a beautifully worn vintage space (the former Odessa diner) and supplements its cult quinoa-chickpea burger with ever-changing, freewheeling sides — roasted sweet potatoes, stuffed cabbage, spicy lentils — that feel more like avant-garde jazz riffs than bar food. The gelato and tapioca pearl pie make dessert as essential as the main event.
popular_dishes: Collard Greens Sandwich on sesame focaccia

name: Sushi Noz
description: Chef Nozomu Abe's Edomae omakase on the Upper East Side is as much a sensory environment as it is a meal — guests sit at a 200-year-old hinoki wood counter in a room built without a single nail, breathing cypress-scented air as flawlessly prepared nigiri arrives piece by piece. The obsessive attention to rice temperature and fish aging puts this among the city's most serious sushi counters, starting at $250 per person.
popular_dishes: Bamboo-smoked eel with braising liquid glaze

name: Sushi Ouji
description: Sushi Ouji is a neighborhood omakase in SoHo that punches well above its $129 price point, offering a relaxed, quality-driven counter experience with well-sourced seafood in a comfortable downtown setting. Eater's reviewer called it a solid value play in a city where comparable omakase meals routinely cost twice as much.

name: Taiwanese Gourmet
description: One of Elmhurst's oldest and most dependable Taiwanese restaurants, this no-frills dining room delivers a vast menu of Taiwanese classics with speed, skill, and perpetually refilled cups of hot tea. The kitchen handles everything from fragrant fly's head to funky fried stinky tofu, making it an ideal spot for a casual group feast — bring cash.
popular_dishes: Fly's Head (minced pork with basil and black bean)

name: Temple Canteen
description: Founded in 1993 in the basement of Flushing's Ganesh temple, this strictly vegetarian South Indian canteen serves some of the most authentic dosas, uttapam, and idlis in New York City at remarkable prices. Diners remove their shoes to eat, and are welcome to visit the Hindu temple upstairs before or after their meal.

name: Thai Diner
description: The spiritual successor to the beloved Uncle Boons, Thai Diner occupies Nolita's former Odessa diner and serves a near-flawless menu that bridges Northern Thai curries and Bangkok wok-fries with gleefully riffed diner classics like Thai disco fries drenched in massaman curry. The sparkly bamboo-walled room, big booths, and swinging kitchen doors complete the enchantment.
popular_dishes: Thai Disco Fries (crinkle-cut fries with massaman curry and peanuts)
Thai Diner Egg Sandwich on sai oua roti

name: Third Falcon
description: A relaxed French-American neighborhood bar-restaurant on Fort Greene's Myrtle Avenue strip, turning out confidently executed bistro food — steak frites, roast chicken, oysters — in a warm, unpretentious room that feels equally suited to a glass of wine at the bar or a proper dinner. It has become a go-to anchor for the surrounding brownstone neighborhood.

name: Torrisi
description: Rich Torrisi's grand Italian-American flagship occupies a vaulted, artwork-filled room inside the landmark Puck Building, serving a menu that weaves together the city's immigrant food traditions — from red-sauce classics to Chinatown influences and Jewish deli nods — with Michelin-starred precision. Dining room reservations open 30 days out on Resy; the bar counter takes walk-ins.

name: Trinciti Roti Shop
description: A beloved Trinidadian counter-service roti shop in South Ozone Park serving the robust flavors of Trinidad and Tobago — warm, freshly made dhalpuri roti folded around curried fillings like goat, chicken, or channa (chickpeas). It draws a loyal community crowd for its honest prices and unapologetically authentic cooking.

name: Txikito
description: Alex Raij and Eder Montero's Chelsea gem has quietly pioneered authentic Basque cooking in New York since 2008, offering a menu heavy on seafood, offal, and beans that adheres faithfully to the Basque home tradition rather than the Spanish tapas shorthand most New Yorkers know. Small plates are modestly priced, and the txakoli wine list is among the city's best.
popular_dishes: Txipiron encebollado (squid ribbons with sweet onion)
Arraultza (canape of chorizo and quail egg)

name: Una Pizza Napoletana
description: Anthony Mangieri's homecoming Neapolitan pizzeria on the Lower East Side, now in a larger, sunlit space, serves a focused menu of wood-fired, 12-inch pies made from long-fermented dough alongside natural wine and Italian-inspired small plates crafted by partners Jeremiah Stone and Fabian von Hauske. Each pie is a simple, artisan statement — $25 for a crust that rivals anything in Naples.

name: Via Carota
description: Rita Sodi and Jody Williams's perpetually buzzy West Village osteria serves seasonal Italian food of quiet, timeless appeal — whole fried rabbit, svizzerina beef patty, and a legendary insalata verde that has become one of the city's most-copied dishes. Walk-ins are always welcome, though waits can stretch long on weekends; the setting, framed by Grove Street's plane trees, is among the most beautiful in New York.

name: Village Café
description: A new Azerbaijani restaurant in Gravesend that opened in 2025, bringing the flavors of the South Caucasus — fragrant lamb kebabs, pomegranate-laced salads, and slow-braised plov (rice pilaf) — to Brooklyn's southern tip. The unpretentious setting and generous portions have quickly made it a neighborhood favorite for the area's Azerbaijani and Central Asian communities.

name: White Bear
description: This tiny, cash-only Flushing dumpling shop is famed across the city for a single menu item: the No. 6, a dozen pork-and-chive wontons in a volcanic chili oil sauce that has inspired pilgrimages and long lines for years. The cramped room seats barely a dozen people, but no one lingers — it's in, eat, out, and completely satisfied.
popular_dishes: No. 6: pork wontons in chili oil (dozen)

name: Yoon Haeundae Galbi
description: Chef Bobby Yoon's Koreatown Korean BBQ carries a multi-generational story — the short-rib cutting technique was developed by Yoon's grandfather at his Busan restaurant — lending a personal depth rarely found in the neighborhood's more anonymous grill houses. The polished room, creative cocktail list, and unusually generous portions set it apart from its densely packed K-town neighbors.
popular_dishes: Galbi (short rib cut with proprietary Busan technique)
Seafood tteokbokki (rice cakes with shrimp, squid, mussels)

name: Zaab Zaab
description: Elmhurst's Michelin Bib Gourmand Isaan Thai restaurant serves the fiery, funky flavors of Thailand's northeast — duck larb pounded with galangal and toasted rice powder, a gaeng om herb curry with beef shank that Time Out called the city's best new soup — in a tiny, mural-ceilinged room open daily until 4am. Chef Aniwat Khotsopa's heat-forward cooking is not for the faint of palate.
popular_dishes: Larb ped Udon (minced duck with galangal and fried skin)
Moo tod pla ra (fermented fish sauce-marinated fried pork belly)
